They split an update in two: an urgent render that shows the keystroke at once, and a background render of the slow part that starts right away and is thrown out whenever newer input arrives. A debounce only moves the moment a blocking render happens, and it's still the right tool for cutting network requests, which deferring doesn't do.
A support dashboard filters 3,000 tickets as an agent types, and every keystroke re-renders the whole list, so typing stutters. The first fix is a 300 ms
. Now nothing moves until the agent pauses, even on a fast laptop, and when the list finally renders, the next keystroke still freezes until it's done. The second fix, after someone reads that
is "React's built-in debounce", makes typing smooth. Then the same developer uses it for the search API and is surprised that the server logs still show one request per keystroke.
are React's debounce. They hold an update back for some fixed amount of time, so fewer renders, and fewer requests, happen while the user types.

It's easy to see why. From the outside the result looks the same: the input moves and the list catches up a moment later. React's own docs say the deferred value "lags behind", which sounds like a timer. Both tools get recommended for the same search box over the same slow list, and a name like "transition" suggests something scheduled for later, like
. The half that's true: both postpone work the user doesn't need this very millisecond. What differs is what decides when that work runs, and whether it can be stopped once it has started.
makes React render twice. First comes an urgent render with the new
but the old deferred value, so the input shows the keystroke right away. Then React tries a background render with the new value for the slow part.
There's no delay between the two. The reference says it directly:

causes no fixed delay, and React starts the background render as soon as the first one finishes. On a powerful laptop the list catches up almost instantly. On a slow phone it lags behind in proportion to how slow the device is. You never pick a number, so you never pick the wrong one.
The background render can be thrown away
This is the part a debounce can't copy. The deferred background render can be interrupted, and so can a

. If the agent types another letter while React is halfway through rendering the list for "ref", React drops that work, handles the keystroke, and starts again with "refu". It always works toward the latest value.

A debounce doesn't make rendering interruptible; it only postpones it. When the timer fires, React renders 3,000 rows in one go, and a keystroke that arrives meanwhile waits. React's docs call debouncing and throttling

for exactly this reason. And if someone types faster than the list can render, the deferred list only updates after they stop typing. That looks like a debounce, but it falls out of interruption, not a timer.

One rule trips people up: a Transition can't update the state that controls a text input, because the input has to reflect the keystroke synchronously. So keep two pieces of state, one urgent for the field and one updated in a Transition for everything that reads it:
Deferring changes when React renders, not what your code does. The reference states that

doesn't by itself prevent extra network requests: a search box that fetches per query still fetches per keystroke. If the expensive work isn't rendering, like a request or an analytics call, a debounce is still the right tool, and React's docs note you can use both together: debounce the request, defer the render. One bonus when the list suspends while loading: with a deferred value, users keep seeing the old results instead of the Suspense fallback.
